title: Against gods made with hands
source_text: Τὰ δὲ περὶ τῆς εἰδωλολατρείας ὡς ἴδια τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου ἐκτιθέμενος καὶ ὑποκατασκευάζει λέγων αὐτοὺς διὰ τοῦτο μὴ νομίζειν αὐτοὺς χειροποιήτους θεοὺς, ἐπεὶ μὴ εὔλογόν ἐστι τὰ ὑπὸ φαυλοτάτων δημιουργῶν καὶ μοχθηρῶν τὸ ἦθος εἰργασμένα εἶναι θεοὺς, πολλάκις καὶ ὑπὸ ἀδίκων ἀνθρώπων κατασκευασθέντα. ἐν τοῖς ἑξῆς οὖν θέλων αὐτὸ κοινοποιῆσαι ὡς οὐ πρῶτον ὑπὸ τούτου εὑρεθὲν ἐκτίθεται Ἡρακλείτου λέξιν τὴν λέγουσαν· „ὅμοια, ὡς εἴ τις τοῖς δόμοις λεσχηνεύοιτο, ποιεῖν τοὺς προσιόντας ὡς θεοῖς τοῖς ἀψύχοις.“ οὐκοῦν καὶ περὶ τούτου λεκτέον ὅτι ὁμοίως τῷ ἄλλῳ ἠθικῷ τόπῳ ἐγκατεσπάρησαν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἔννοιαι, ἀφ᾿ ὧν καὶ ὁ Ἡράκλειτος καὶ εἴ τις ἄλλος Ἑλλήνων ἢ βαρβάρων τοῦτ᾿ ἐνενόησε κατασκευάσαι. ἐκτίθεται γὰρ καὶ Πέρσας τοῦτο φρονοῦντας, παρατιθέμενος Ἡρόδοτον ἱστοροῦντα αὐτό. προσθήσομεν δὲ καὶ ἡμεῖς ὅτι καὶ Ζήνων ὁ Κιτιεὺς ἐν τῇ Πολιτείᾳ φησίν· „ἱερά τε οἰκοδομεῖν οὐδὲν δεήσει· ἱερὸν γὰρ οὐδὲν χρὴ νομίζειν οὐδὲ πολλοῦ ἄξιον καὶ ἅγιον, οἰκοδόμων τε ἔργον καὶ βαναύσων.“ σαφὲς οὖν ὅτι καὶ περὶ τούτου τοῦ δόγματος γέγραπται „ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις“ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γράμμασι θεοῦ τὸ πρακτέον.
pass_a_gloss: The things about idolatry (εἰδωλολατρεία), setting them out (ἐκτίθημι) as peculiar (ἴδιος) to those from the teaching (λόγος), he also supports by argument (ὑποκατασκευάζω), saying that they for this reason do not consider (νομίζω) handmade (χειροποίητος) gods, since it is not reasonable (εὔλογος) that the things worked by the most worthless (φαυλότατος) craftsmen (δημιουργός), wicked (μοχθηρός) in character (ἦθος), are gods, often also made by unjust (ἄδικος) men. In what follows then, wishing to make it common (κοινοποιέω) as not first discovered (εὑρίσκω) by this, he sets out a saying (λέξις) of Heraclitus: 'like, as if someone were to chat (λεσχηνεύω) with houses (δόμοι), do those who approach (πρόσειμι) lifeless (ἄψυχος) things as gods.' So about this too it must be said that, like the other ethical topic, notions (ἔννοιαι) were sown in men, from which Heraclitus and any other of Greeks or barbarians conceived (ἐννοέω) to argue (κατασκευάζω) this. For he also sets out the Persians thinking (φρονέω) this, citing (παρατίθημι) Herodotus reporting (ἱστορέω) it. We too will add that Zeno of Citium in the Republic (Πολιτεία) says: 'there will be no need (δεήσει) to build (οἰκοδομέω) temples (ἱερά); for one must consider no temple (ἱερόν) of much worth (πολλοῦ ἄξιος) and holy (ἅγιος), the work of builders (οἰκοδόμοι) and mechanics (βάναυσοι).' Clear then that about this doctrine too the thing to be done (τὸ πρακτέον) is written 'in the hearts' of men in letters (γράμματα) of God.
pass_b_english: Setting out our views on idolatry as something peculiar to those who follow our teaching, he even supplies an argument for them, saying that for this reason they do not believe in gods made with hands: it is not reasonable that things made by the basest of craftsmen, men of wicked character, should be gods, when they have often been fashioned by unjust men as well.

Then, in what follows, wishing to make this a common view, on the ground that it was not first discovered by our teaching, he sets out a saying of Heraclitus: “Those who approach lifeless things as gods act like someone chatting with houses” (Heraclitus, fragment 5). So about this too we must say that, as with the rest of moral teaching, notions were sown in men, and from them Heraclitus, and any other Greek or barbarian, thought of arguing this point. For he also points out that the Persians hold this view, citing Herodotus, who reports it (Herodotus, Histories 1.131).

We too will add that Zeno of Citium also says in his Republic: “There will be no need to build temples; for no temple ought to be thought of great worth or holy, since it is the work of builders and mechanics.” It is clear, then, that with this doctrine too, what must be done has been written “in the hearts” of men (Romans 2:15) in God's own writing.

choices.choice: Celsus is reported indirectly in the first paragraph; the Heraclitus and Zeno lines are direct quotations and take quotation marks. Heraclitus is fragment B5 in Diels-Kranz; the Greek word order puts 'like' first ('ὅμοια ... ποιεῖν τοὺς προσιόντας'), turned into natural English. Herodotus 1.131 reports that the Persians set up no statues, temples or altars. Zeno's Republic fragment is usually collected in von Arnim, SVF 1.264; not added inline. 'Written in the hearts' (ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις) again draws on Romans 2:15; 'letters of God' may also recall 2 Corinthians 3:3 (written on tablets of human hearts), possible only. 'χειροποιήτους θεούς' ('gods made with hands') is Celsus's phrase as reported; it resembles Acts 17:24 and Isaiah 46:6 language but is not cited, since the words are Celsus's. Zeno: 'ἱερὸν οὐδὲν χρὴ νομίζειν' can also be parsed 'nothing should be thought sacred ... that is the work of builders'; the sense (temples, as builders' work, are not of great worth or holy) is the same either way.
Recast the wordy opening 'As for what concerns idolatry, he sets it out' as 'Setting out our views on idolatry ...' to follow the participle ἐκτιθέμενος
'worst of craftsmen' to 'basest of craftsmen' (φαυλότατοι means morally base, not unskilled)
'as if it were not first discovered' to 'on the ground that it was not first discovered' (ὡς gives Celsus's reason; 'as if' wrongly hinted at falsehood)
'thought to argue' to 'thought of arguing' (ἐνενόησε κατασκευάσαι)
'sets out that the Persians think so' to 'points out that the Persians hold this view'
'in letters from God' to 'in God's own writing' (γράμμασι θεοῦ are written characters, not epistles; ties to ch. 4)
Confirmed Heraclitus DK 22 B5 (δόμοισι λεσχηνεύοιτο), Herodotus 1.131 (Persians set up no statues, temples or altars), Romans 2:15
